events.title: Innocent III approves the Trinitarian Order
events.shortBlurb: By a bull of 17 December 1198 Innocent III approved the young Order of the Most Holy Trinity, vowed to the ransom of Christian captives…
body: St. John of Matha, with the hermit St. Felix of Valois for his companion, had gathered at Cerfroid, in the diocese of Meaux, a brotherhood unlike any then in the Church: its end was the redemption of Christian captives from the hands of the Muslims, by ransom, charity, and mercy.

Innocent III, though little in favor of new orders, as the Catholic Encyclopedia observes, granted his approbation to the enterprise in a bull of 17 December 1198 — the Operante divinae dispositionis clementiae — confirming the rule that John had brought to Rome.

That rule directed that the revenues of every house be divided into three parts: one for the brothers, one for the support of the poor, and one for the ransom of captives; each house was to comprise seven brothers, one of whom should be superior. The pope took the order under his protection, and the church of San Tommaso in Formis at Rome became its chief house. The Trinitarians, the first religious order vowed to the freeing of prisoners, spread through Europe and Spain in the later Middle Ages.
